toolStatus: Opened fine: Drowned in Sound, Medium (MJ O'Neill), Steel for Brains (Tumblr), Fused Magazine, Spectrum Culture, Hot Press, Far Out (2 pages), The Current, Wikipedia (Pavement). Not opened: the AV Club Zak Sally URL redirected to the AV Club homepage. Every web.archive.org URL I built or copied (AV Club, and the CrackedMachine archive from Wikipedia footnote 12) was refused with 'not in any prior search or fetch result', and web_search did not surface them. The AOL syndication of the Independent LCD piece (aol.com/lcd-soundsystem-album-changed-music-063000380.html) returned a client error; its text showed only in a search result, so I did not use it as evidence. All 13 links are covered. Search results were noisy, so most of the work was fetch-and-read.

bon-iver>tom-waits.note: The PopMatters 2008 claim is not on the PopMatters page, as the last checker found, and I found no PopMatters source. The only first-person Waits mention I found is The Current's transcript of Justin Vernon on Tuesdays with Lazerbeak (Jay Gabler, 22 Apr 2020). Vernon says: "my parents were great music fans like the standard kinda Dylan, Janis Joplin kind of house but also we had some Mingus records and some – John Prine was our biggest kind of favorite thing and definitely some weirder Waits – Tom Waits stuff – and Janis stuff in general." That only says Waits records were in the childhood house. It does not say Waits shaped his music, and the same page names John Prine as the major inspiration. Proposal: remove the link, or keep it only as a weak first-person 'grew up around' entry if household listening counts. Other pages I read only mention Vernon covering Waits live or collaborators who played with Waits, which is not influence.

four-tet>aphex-twin.found: I think there’s nothing more magical, though, than when someone makes something that is truly experimental and truly kind of natural and human at the same time. Something like Aphex Twin’s ‘Windowlicker’, for example.
four-tet>aphex-twin.note: Hebden's own words (2011, MJ O'Neill on Medium) hold up Windowlicker as the ideal he admires most ('the absolute grail'), but never say it shaped his music; the old 1999-remix corroboration isn't influence. Propose: keep as first-person fandom if admiration from a working producer counts, else remove.

have-a-nice-life>dead-kennedys.found: Yeah, the default music of my youth was the Dead Kennedys, Descendents, Op Iy.
have-a-nice-life>dead-kennedys.citation: Tim Macuga to Steel for Brains ("The Big Gloom - A Conversation With Have a Nice Life", 21 February 2014), asked which bands from his youth had the biggest impact on him: "Yeah, the default music of my youth was the Dead Kennedys, Descendents, Op Iy."
have-a-nice-life>dead-kennedys.note: This is Macuga's own words, so the tier is upgraded from reported to first-person. The page spells it 'Op Iy' (Operation Ivy). The question asked about youth music with the biggest impact. Dan Barrett's separate answer says the bands directly influencing HANL were not what he listened to growing up.

have-a-nice-life>descendents.note: Same page and sentence as the Dead Kennedys link.

lcd-soundsystem>the-birthday-party.found: I love things like The Stranglers and The Birthday Party, where the bass is just this monster.
lcd-soundsystem>the-birthday-party.citation: James Murphy to Fused Magazine (2005 interview, republished online 16 January 2024): "I love things like The Stranglers and The Birthday Party, where the bass is just this monster."
lcd-soundsystem>the-birthday-party.note: This replaces the Independent citation, which I could not open. A search result for the Independent US piece (Mark Beaumont, 2025, syndicated on AOL) did show the sentence calling Murphy an 'avid student of the likes of The Birthday Party, Can, The Velvet Underground', but the AOL page errored on fetch. The original independent.co.uk URL never appeared in results. If you keep the Independent citation, the AOL URL is https://www.aol.com/lcd-soundsystem-album-changed-music-063000380.html. This Fused quote is Murphy praising the band while talking about bass players, not an explicit 'shaped me' statement.

lcd-soundsystem>velvet-underground.found: For me, The Fall, along with The Velvet Underground, are the best rock ‘n’ roll bands of all time.
lcd-soundsystem>velvet-underground.citation: James Murphy to Fused Magazine (2005 interview, republished online 16 January 2024): "For me, The Fall, along with The Velvet Underground, are the best rock ‘n’ roll bands of all time."
lcd-soundsystem>velvet-underground.note: This is first-person fandom, and in context he is explaining why he'd rather sound like Mark E Smith than Mick Jagger. The Fall are his main point, with the Velvets grouped alongside. The Independent version (see the Birthday Party link) was seen only in a search result, not opened.

low>velvet-underground.note: retry5: the AV Club Zak Sally interview (archive 2010/2012/2016 copies) has no Velvet Underground or Sister Ray; the Stereogum line and the MOJO 12:38 quote weren't found by two chat searches. Sparhawk's Quietus Baker's Dozen has no VU pick.

modest-mouse>built-to-spill.found: That paragraph-above nod to DCFC and Modest Mouse is entirely relevant for another reason, too, as both Isaac Brock and Ben Gibbard have cited Built To Spill as a great influence on their arena-filling acts.
modest-mouse>built-to-spill.citation: Mike Diver, in Drowned in Sound's review of Built To Spill's You In Reverse, wrote that Isaac Brock and Ben Gibbard "have cited Built To Spill as a great influence on their arena-filling acts."
modest-mouse>built-to-spill.note: This replaces the Pitchfork/Richardson 2006 citation, which I could not locate. The page names Brock as having cited Built To Spill as an influence, so it is a publication reporting Brock's own statement, with no direct quote from him. The page has no visible date; the score line is credited to Mike Diver. For a first-person alternative, Stereogum's Premature Evaluation piece on Built To Spill's When The Wind Forgets Your Name (stereogum.com/2198651/built-to-spill-when-the-wind-forgets-your-name/reviews/premature-evaluation) says Brock's guitar style was 'shaped by seeing Martsch play', quoting him to the LA Times that it was 'all really like Treepeople influence'. I read that only as a search result, not opened.

pavement>the-replacements.found: I first spoke to Pavement back in the Slanted And Enchanted days. Squatting outside the Boardwalk on a warm summer evening, Scott Kannberg aka Spiral Stairs told me how he preferred the Replacements to the Fall.
pavement>the-replacements.citation: The Cracked Machine fanzine's Pavement interview recalls meeting the band in the Slanted and Enchanted days, when Scott Kannberg "told me how he preferred the Replacements to the Fall."
pavement>the-replacements.note: Wikipedia's footnote 12; opened via the Internet Archive (2001 copy). The writer's paraphrase, so reported.

sonic-youth>this-heat.found: Though active for only a very short time, the influence of This Heat's groundbreaking experimentation was immediately visible in the pre-industrial grit of Public Image, Ltd., Sonic Youth's early skronk, and Glenn Branca's wiry wall-of-noise symphonies.
sonic-youth>this-heat.citation: Fred Thomas, in AllMusic's This Heat biography: "the influence of This Heat's groundbreaking experimentation was immediately visible in... Sonic Youth's early skronk."

the-cranberries>siouxsie-and-the-banshee.found: As admirers of The Cure, Echo and the Bunnymen, Siouxsie and the Banshees, Joy Division and New Order, the quartet called on Stephen Street, who had produced Strangeways, Here We Come for The Smiths, ultimately the influence strongest for The Cranberries.
the-cranberries>siouxsie-and-the-banshee.citation: John L. Murphy, "Revisit: The Cranberries: Everybody Else Is Doing it, So Why Can’t We?", Spectrum Culture (12 November 2018), described the band as "admirers of The Cure, Echo and the Bunnymen, Siouxsie and the Banshees, Joy Division and New Order."
the-cranberries>siouxsie-and-the-banshee.note: This replaces the O'Riordan 'yodeling' claim, which is not on the Forbes page the last checker opened, and I found no source for it. The new source is a reviewer's statement about the whole band, not a quote from O'Riordan. The page shows italics on the album title, which I left out of 'found'.

yeah-yeah-yeahs>sonic-youth.found: I tried so hard to be cool the first time we were introduced but no, I dorked out completely! How can you not when they’re the godfathers and godmother of experimental music?
yeah-yeah-yeahs>sonic-youth.citation: Karen O to Hot Press (Stuart Clark, 13 October 2006), naming Sonic Youth when asked which of her heroes she had met: "I tried so hard to be cool the first time we were introduced but no, I dorked out completely! How can you not when they’re the godfathers and godmother of experimental music?"
yeah-yeah-yeahs>sonic-youth.note: The Wikipedia 'inspirations' list and the NY Magazine footnote do not carry this, as the last checker found. This is the replacement: Karen O's own words, answering the interviewer's question 'which of Karen’s heroes has she actually met?' with 'Sonic Youth'. It is hero-worship fandom, not an explicit stylistic-influence statement, so downgrade to decide if you want the latter.

yeah-yeah-yeahs>the-birthday-party.found: She has mentioned everybody from ESG to the Birthday Party to Nina Simone, and yes, Siouxsie Sioux as influences.
yeah-yeah-yeahs>the-birthday-party.citation: Far Out Magazine, in "How the Grateful Dead soundtracked Karen O’s teenage years", states that Karen O has named the Birthday Party among her influences.
yeah-yeah-yeahs>the-birthday-party.note: This is a publication's own unsourced statement about Karen O; the page gives no quote or interview for the Birthday Party, and no date is visible. Weak corroboration: Far Out's piece on the band's BBC 6 Music artist residency (https://faroutmagazine.co.uk/yeah-yeah-yeahs-early-inspirations/) lists The Birthday Party under 'The early influences on the Yeah Yeah Yeahs', but only as a bare list item with no comment from the band, so I did not use it as the main evidence. Replaces the NY Magazine/Wikipedia citation, which does not name the Birthday Party.
